@6

Civil procedure
-- Discovery -- Exception to solicitor-client

privilege which
exists with respect to communications in

furtherance of
unlawful conduct applying to communications

perpetrating
tortious conduct which may become subject of civil

proceedings.

The plaintiff
was the original head of the defendant school.

He brought an
action against the defendants for damages for

breach of
contract, intentional or negligent infliction of

emotional harm,
negligence, breach of trust and breach of

confidence. A
claim was also advanced on behalf of the

plaintiff's son
alleging that the defendants were negligent, in

breach of
contract, in breach of trust and in breach of

confidence in
respect of their conduct towards him and that

they
intentionally or negligently inflicted emotional harm on

him. It was
alleged that the defendants' actions were

undertaken with
malice, dishonesty and subterfuge. An e-mail

message which was
sent by one of the defendants to the lawyer

retained to act
on behalf of the defendants was inadvertently

disclosed to the
plaintiffs after the litigation commenced.

When the
plaintiffs refused to return copies of the e-mail, the

defendants
brought a motion for an order for its return. The

Master ruled that
the e-mail was covered by solicitor-client

privilege and
granted the order. The plaintiffs appealed.

Held, the
appeal should be allowed.

The e-mail fell
within the exception to solicitor-client

privilege which
applies to communications in furtherance of

unlawful conduct.
There is no reason why this exception should

not include communications
perpetrating tortious conduct that

may become the
subject of civil proceedings. This case involved

the assertion
that various intentional torts were committed

against the
plaintiffs. The e-mail communication might show

that the
defendants, or at least the author of the e-mail

[page512]
message, intended to inflict emotional harm on the

plaintiffs. As
the e-mail was not privileged and was relevant,

it should have
been disclosed to the plaintiffs.

APPEAL from an
order granting a motion for the return of a

document.

@8

Robert Zigler,
for plaintiffs.

Jess Bush, for
defendants.

@7

PERELL J.: --

Introduction and
Overview

[
1
] Perhaps the
most excruciating duty of a civil litigation

lawyer is
preparing an affidavit of documents. This appeal by

the plaintiffs
from the order of Master Albert dated March 15,

2006 examines why
this is necessarily so.

[
2
] In our
contemporary world of information excess, apart

from the ever
more onerous burden of collecting documents from

their myriad of
technological resting places, when preparing an

affidavit of
documents, a lawyer is confronted with many

difficult
questions. Does the document have a semblance of

relevance to the
action as pleaded? If the document is relevant

to the issues in
the proceedings, then is it subject to a

privilege? And
there are many privileges, including lawyer and

client privilege,
litigation privilege, a special relationship

or Wigmore
privilege, settlement communication privilege,

spousal
privilege, self-incrimination privilege, public

interest
immunity, informant privilege, judicial privilege, and

privilege
[page514] granted by statute. And the categories of

privilege are not
closed:
Smith v. Jones
,
1999 CanLII 674 (SCC)
,
[1999] 1 S.C.R. 455
,

1999 CanLII 674 (SCC)
,
[1999] S.C.J. No.
15
. If the document is privileged then is

it caught by an
exception to privilege; for example, the crime

or fraud
exception, or the innocence at stake exception, or the

public safety
exception? Or, if the document is privileged, has

the privilege
been waived advertently or inadvertently? And if

the privilege has
been waived inadvertently, can the privilege

be reasserted?

[
3
] The lawyer
has a duty to ensure that his or her client

makes the
disclosure required by the
Rules of Civil Procedure
,

R.R.O. 1990, Reg.
194
, but at the same time, the lawyer has a

duty to maintain
the confidences and to protect and not

disclose the
privileged communications and documents of his or

her client. Thus,
in a context of an adversary system, where

the lawyer has a
duty to the client and a duty to the

administration of
justice, the lawyer is simultaneously under

the excruciating
pull of a duty of disclosure and a duty of

non-disclosure.

[
4
] Where a
document adds unfavourable colour or is

embarrassing or
is an invasion of the client's personal or

commercial
privacy and it is intertwined with possibly

privileged
information, it is an excruciatingly difficult

judgment call
about whether the document should be disclosed.

[
5
] With the
greatest respect, in the immediate case, my own

judgment call is
that the master erred by ruling that a

document that had
been inadvertently disclosed in the

reproductions of
documents from the defendants' affidavit of

documents was
privileged and ought therefore to be returned to

the defendants.
In my opinion, in the circumstances of this

case, the
document was an exception to privilege because it was

arguably in
furtherance of unlawful conduct and that is an

exception to
privilege.

[
6
] Because the
document was not privileged, the fact that

the document was
inadvertently disclosed becomes immaterial.

Also with the
greatest respect to the lawyers acting for the

defendants, who,
I have no doubt, were acting honourably and in

good faith in
preparing or supervising the preparation of their

client's
affidavit of documents, the document ought to have

been disclosed in
the first place.

[
7
] In every
other respect, I would have dismissed this

appeal, but it appears
that the in furtherance of unlawful

conduct exception
was not brought to the master's attention.

All she says
about the topic in her endorsement is in para. 25

where she states:
"Dublin wants the document produced because

it contains
pejorative statements (without using names) which,

counsel argues,
would provide assistance as to the board's

state of mind.
That is not a sufficient reason to undermine

solicitor client
privilege." [page515]

[
8
] However, in
my opinion, there is more to this matter.

Therefore, for
the reasons that follow, and because it is my

conclusion that
an exception to privilege does apply, I am

granting the
plaintiffs' appeal and ordering that what was

known as
production 72 to be produced to them.

[
9
] To explain
my conclusion will require four steps. First,

as a part of this
introduction, I will briefly discuss the

standard of
appellate review. Second, I will describe the

parties and some
of the factual circumstances. I believe that

this can be done
relatively briefly because an account of some

of the details
can be postponed until I discuss the other

grounds of appeal
later in my judgment. Third, I will describe

the law of
privilege that I believe is applicable to the facts

in this case and
determinative of the appeal. Fourth, I will

address the other
grounds of appeal raised.

[
10
] Turning to
the matter of appellate review, on an appeal

from a master's
order that is a matter of discretion, the court

will only
interfere if the master was clearly wrong or if he or

she exercised
discretion based on wrong principles or under a

misapprehension
of the facts: Bank of Nova Scotia v. Liberty

Mutual Insurance
Co.
(2003),
2003 CanLII 35171 (ON SCDC)
,
67 O.R. (3d) 699
, [2003] O.J. No.

4474 (Div. Ct.);
Marleen Investments Ltd. v. McBride (1979), 23

O.R. (2d) 125,

1979 CanLII 1895 (ON HCJ)
,
[1979] O.J. No. 4050 (H.C.J.)
; Woodheath

Developments Ltd.
v. Goldman
(2003),
2003 CanLII 46735 (ON SCDC)
,
66 O.R. (3d) 731
, [2003]

O.J. No. 3440
(Div. Ct.); Fotwe v. Citadel General Assurance

Co.,
2005 CanLII 5470 (ON SCDC)
,
[2005] O.J.
No. 827
,
25 C.P.C. (6th) 220 (Div. Ct.)
.

[
11
] Where the
master's order concerns a question of law and

the outcome of
the question is vital to the disposition of the

law suit, the
court will interfere if the master errs: Bank of

Nova Scotia v.
Liberty Mutual Insurance Co., supra. In my

opinion, in the
case at bar, the outcome of the privilege

question is of
sufficient importance to the possible outcome of

the litigation
that correctness is the appropriate standard of

appellate review.

Factual
Background

[
12
] I take the
factual background from the statement of

claim and the
affidavit material filed on the motion.

[
13
] The
plaintiff Dr. Max Dublin was the original head of

the defendant
Montessori Jewish Day School of Toronto. His

infant son, the
plaintiff Ephraim Dublin, was a student at the

school.
Unfortunately, Ephraim suffers from a medical problem

that produces
occasional incidents of incontinence.

[
14
] The
defendant Montessori Jewish Day School of Toronto is

a not-for-profit
corporation without share capital under the

Corporations Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. C.38
. Its members are the

parents [page516]
of students attending the school, and they

elect a board of
directors. Dr. Dublin was ex officio a member

of the board of
directors.

[
15
] In October
2003, Dr. Dublin took a leave of absence from

his post as head
to recover from depression.

[
16
] During Dr.
Dublin's absence, it is alleged that the

defendant school,
the defendant Patti Nashman, who had just

recently been
appointed chair of its board of directors, and

the defendant Kim
Pasternak, who was a member of the board of

directors and
temporary acting head of the school, were

negligent, in
breach of contract, in breach of trust, in breach

of confidence and
that they intentionally or negligently

inflicted
emotional harm on Ephraim. It is alleged that in

response to his
incontinence problem he was mistreated,

publicly
ridiculed, embarrassed and illegally suspended from

the school.

[
17
] During Dr.
Dublin's absence, it is also alleged that the

board of
directors of the school led by Ms. Nashman began a

process that led
to Dr. Dublin's allegedly wrongful dismissal

in May of 2004.
Dr. Dublin alleges that he was wrongfully

dismissed from
employment, and he claims damages for

intentional or
negligent infliction of emotional harm,

negligence,
breach of trust and breach of confidence. It is

alleged that the
defendants' actions were undertaken with

malice,
dishonesty and subterfuge.

[
18
] Dr.
Dublin's leave of absence began on October 7, 2003,

which was also a
day where the board of directors had a

meeting. At the
board meeting, the members discussed Dr.

Dublin's leave of
absence and also pending negotiations with

respect to his
employment contract. The board members

authorized Ms.
Nashman to communicate with legal counsel about

these and other
matters.

[
19
] The board
meeting was not in camera, and the minutes of

the meeting
reveal that Ms. Nashman was authorized to contact

counsel about
conflicts of interest in the school's

infrastructure
and questions arising from Dr. Dublin's absence

as head of the
school.

[
20
] Shortly
after the October 7, 2003 board of directors

meeting, Ms.
Nashman contacted Mr. David Steinberg, a lawyer at

the law firm of
Heenan Blaikie, LL.P. Mr. Steinberg was a

longstanding
friend of Ms. Nashman. His firm was retained to

act on behalf of
the school. Ms. Nashman and at least three

other board
members met with Mr. Steinberg and his colleague

Mr. Henry
Dinsdale with respect to matters concerning Dr.

Dublin's
employment and his medical leave of absence. A letter

was prepared to
be delivered to Dr. Dublin.

[
21
] On or
about October 26, 2003, Ms. Nashman sent an e-mail

message to Mr.
Steinberg. Ms. Nashman sent the e-mail using the

e-mail account of
her husband who is not a member of the

[page517] board
and the e-mail message alludes to the

involvement of
third parties in its composition.

[
22
] The
defendants claim that the exchange of e-mail between

Ms. Nashman and
Mr. Steinberg is privileged as a lawyer and

client
communication to obtain legal advice. The Dublins, who

much later came
to see a copy of the message, contend that it

is evidence of
the defendants' malice and bad faith.

[
23
] Dr. Dublin
resumed work in January 2004, and he also

resumed an active
role on the board of directors of the school,

but he was
dismissed in May 2004.

[
24
] Dr. Dublin
did not know about the e-mail message when

this action
commenced on October 19, 2004. The e-mail message,

however, was
inadvertently disclosed during the ensuing

litigation, and
when the plaintiffs refused to return copies of

the message, the
defendants brought an interlocutory motion for

the return of the
e-mail. The motion came before Master Albert,

who inspected the
e-mail message (as I have) and ruled that it

was privileged
and should be returned.

[
25
] Dr. Dublin
and Ephraim, whose litigation guardian is his

mother, Julia
Dublin, appeal the order of the master.

Privilege and
Exceptions to Lawyer-and-Client Privilege

[
26
]
Lawyer-and-client privilege concerns communications

between a lawyer
and his or her client. It is a fundamental

right and a
substantive rule of law: Canada v. Solosky, [1980]

1979 CanLII 9 (SCC)
,
1 S.C.R. 821
,

[1979] S.C.J. No. 130
; Desc“teaux v. Mierzwinski,

1982 CanLII 22 (SCC)
,
[1982] 1 S.C.R.
860
,
[1982] S.C.J. No. 43
;
R. v. McClure
,

2001 SCC 14 (CanLII)
,
[2001] 1 S.C.R.
445
,
[2001] S.C.J. No. 13
; Lavallee, Rackel

& Heintz v.
Canada (Attorney General),
2002 SCC 61 (CanLII)
,
[2002] 3 S.C.R. 209
,

2002 SCC 61 (CanLII)
,
[2002] S.C.J. No.
61
.

[
27
] To qualify
for lawyer-and-client privilege, a

communication
must be: (1) between a client and his or her

lawyer who must
be acting in a professional capacity as a

lawyer; (2) given
in the context of obtaining legal advice; and

(3) intended to
be confidential: Desc“teaux v. Mierzwinski,

supra;
R. v.
Campbell
,
1999 CanLII 676 (SCC)
,
[1999] 1 S.C.R. 565
, [1999] S.C.J. No.

16;
Gower v.
Tolko Manitoba Inc.
,
2001 MBCA 11 (CanLII)
,
[2001] M.J. No. 39
, 196

D.L.R. (4th) 716
(C.A.); Wigmore on Evidence, vol. 8

(McNaughton rev.,
1961, para. 2292).

[
28
] In order
to ensure public confidence in the legal system

and the
effectiveness of the privilege, lawyer-and-client

privilege is
categorical and approaches an absolute right,

rather than one
that is decided on a case-by-case basis:

Lavallee, Rackel
& Heintz v. Canada (Attorney General)
, supra;

R. v. McClure
,
supra; Pritchard v. Ontario (Human Rights

Commission),

2004 SCC 31 (CanLII)
,
[2004] 1 S.C.R. 809
,
[2004] S.C.J. No. 16
, affg

(2003),
2003 CanLII 8701 (ON CA)
,
63 O.R.
(3d) 97
,
[2003] O.J. No. 215 (C.A.)
.

[page518]
Exceptions to the lawyer-and-client privilege are

possible, but
their availability is strictly limited.

[
29
] No
privilege is absolute, and there are exceptions to

lawyer-and-client
privilege and the other privileges: Smith v.

Jones, supra. If
a client seeks guidance from a lawyer to

facilitate
committing a crime or a fraud, the communication

will not be
privileged and it is immaterial whether the lawyer

is a knowing
participant or unwitting dupe of the client.

[
30
] The
classic example of an exception to lawyer-and-client

privilege is R.
v. Cox and Railton
(1884),
14 Q.B.D. 153
, a

stated case in
criminal proceedings. In this case, after

judgment had been
issued against him in civil proceedings for

libel, Railton
executed a bill of sale of his newspaper.

Railton was
convicted of fraudulently conveying his assets to

avoid his
judgment creditor, and the crucial evidence came from

a Mr. Goodman,
the lawyer who had provided Railton with legal

advice that there
had to be a bona fide sale of the property.

It may be noted
that Mr. Goodman's advice itself appears to

have been proper
legal advice.

[
31
] On appeal,
the question for the Court for Crown Cases

Reserved was
whether Goodman's evidence was properly admitted

or whether it
should have been excluded because of lawyer-and-

client privilege.
The case was first argued before five

judges, and then,
because of its importance, re-argued before

ten judges. In
the result, the court upheld the conviction and

ruled that the
evidence was properly admitted.

[
32
] Stephen J.
concluded that if a client attends on a legal

adviser for
advice intended to facilitate or to guide the

client in
committing a crime or fraud, the communication

between the two
is not privileged and can be disclosed by the

lawyer. He stated
that a communication in furtherance of a

criminal purpose
does not come within the ordinary scope of

professional
employment and is not privileged.

[
33
] For the
future crime or fraud exception to apply, it

must be shown
that the client had an illegal purpose in mind

and that the
lawyer either shared that illegal purpose or was

deceived as to
the client's purpose. In other words, the

exception applies
only where the client knows or should have

known that the
intended conduct was unlawful:
R. v. Campbell
,

supra, at paras.
55-61.

[
34
] The
client's intention to commit a wrongful act is the

key determinant
as to whether the communication is privileged:

Goldman, Sachs
& Co. v. Sessions
,
1999 CanLII 5317 (BC SC)
,
[1999] B.C.J. No. 2815
, 38

C.P.C. (4th) 143
(S.C.). In circumstances where the client has

a wrongful
intent, the lawyer, in providing advice that may

facilitate the
illegal activity, is not acting in a

professional
capacity. In contrast, if a lawyer bona fide

communicates
advice about the legality of proposed conduct,

which is a normal
and important [page519] function for a

lawyer, then the
communication is privileged, even if it turns

out that the
lawyer was wrong in advising that the conduct was

legal: the
privilege is not destroyed if the transaction turns

out to be
illegal:
R. v. Campbell
, supra, at paras.
55-61
.

[
35
] I pause
here to note that having to consider the

client's
intention and the nicety of the distinctions being

drawn here
obviously adds to the difficulties of a lawyer

determining
whether a particular communication is privileged

when he or she
prepares an affidavit of documents.

[
36
] The
difficulties are demonstrated by Desc“teaux v.

Mierzwinski,
supra. In this case, it was alleged that Mr.

Ledoux had
falsely stated his income on an application for

legal aid
contrary to
s. 324
of the
Criminal Code
, R.S.C. 1970,

c. C-34. In
furtherance of a criminal investigation, a justice

of the peace
issued a search warrant, and police officers

attended at a
legal aid bureau in Montr‚al to execute the

warrant and to
seize the legal aid application form that

contained
information supplied by Mr. Ledoux about his

financial means.
The application form also contained other

information,
including professional notes from the lawyer

assigned to the case.
An application for certiorari was brought

to assert that
the seized material, which was placed in a

sealed envelope
without examination, was protected by lawyer-

and-client
privilege.

[
37
] Lamer J.,
as he then was, upheld the dismissal of the

application by
the lower courts on the grounds that Mr.

Ledoux's false
communications were not privileged and

appropriate
safeguards were in place to protect the genuinely

privileged
portions of the legal aid application from

disclosure. Lamer
J. stated that confidential communications,

whether they
relate to financial means or to the legal problem

itself, lose that
character if and to the extent that they were

made for the
purpose of obtaining legal advice to facilitate

committing a
crime or if the communications were in themselves

criminal, as was
the situation in the Desc“teaux case.

[
38
] The
authors of Canada's leading evidence text, Sopinka,

Lederman and
Bryant, The Law of Evidence in Canada, 2nd ed.

(Markham, Ont.:
Butterworths, 1999) state in para. 14.58:

"There is no
reason why this exception to the solicitor-

client privilege
should not also include those

communications
made with a view to perpetrating tortuous [sic]

conduct which may
become the subject of criminal proceedings."

[
39
] In my
opinion, there is also no reason why the exception

should not
include communications perpetrating [tortious]

conduct that may
become the subject of civil proceedings.

[
40
]
In

Goldman, Sachs & Co. v. Sessions
, supra, K.J. Smith

J. included
within the scope of conduct that will remove a

communication
from the protection, the tort of abuse of

process, breaches
[page520] of regulatory statutes, breaches of

contract, and
torts and other breaches of duty. See also

Northwest Mettech
Corp. v. Metcon Services Ltd.
, [1997] B.C.J.

No. 2734,
1997 CanLII 3843 (BC SC)
,
78
C.P.R. (3d) 86 (S.C.)
, where it was held that the

crime and fraud
exception may apply where the alleged unlawful

conduct is a
breach of fiduciary duty or a breach of

confidence. It
may be noted that these types of allegations are

made in the case
at bar.

[
41
] K.J. Smith
J. came to his conclusion about the scope of

the exception to
lawyer-and-client privilege by his reading of

Binnie J.'s

judgment in
R. v. Campbell
, supra, which in turn

was an
interpretation of the seminal R. v. Cox and Railton,

supra. In paras.
13 to 15 of his judgment, K.J. Smith J.

discussed Binnie
J.'s judgment and stated:

Binnie J.
went on to observe, in para. 57, that Professor

Wigmore
expressed the view, in Wigmore on Evidence, vol. 8

(McNaughton
Rev. 1961) sec. 2298, at p. 573, that the

exception
applies only where the client seeks the legal

advice for a
knowingly unlawful end. He continued, at para.

58:

Although
the issue has apparently not been directly

considered in the Canadian case law, the Wigmore view

was
subsequently espoused by the authors of "The Future

Crime or
Tort Exception to Communications Privileges"

(1964),
77 Harv. L. Rev. 730, where they state as

follows,
at pp. 730-31:

The
attorney-client privilege has always been subject

to the
qualification that protection is denied to

communications wherein a lawyer's assistance is sought

in
activity that the client knows to constitute a

crime
or tort. [Emphasis per Binnie J.]

The scope of
the "future crimes" exception is circumscribed

on a public
policy basis, as explained at p. 731:

The
knowledge requirement minimizes the effect of the

exception
on proper communications; absent this

requirement legitimate consultations would be inhibited

by the
risk that their subject matter might turn out to

be illegal
and therefore unprivileged. Moreover,

counseling against unfounded claims or illegal projects

is an
important part of the lawyer's function.

After
noting, in para. 59, that this explanation of the

rule is
consistent with its exposition in the context of

crime and
fraud by Lamer J. in Desc“teaux v. Mierzwinski,

1982 CanLII 22 (SCC)
,
[1982] 1
S.C.R. 860
at p. 881
and by Lord Parmoor in

O'Rourke v.
Darbishire,
[1920] A.C. 581 (H.L.)
, at p. 621,

Binnie J.
made it clear that the client's intention is the

pivotal
consideration, quoting with approval from State ex

rel. North
Pacific Lumber Co. v. Unis,
579 P.2d 1291
(Or.

1978) at p.
1295 as follows:

We
approve of the requirement that, in order to invoke

the
exception to the privilege, the proponent of the

evidence
must show that the client, when consulting the

attorney,
knew or should have known that the intended

conduct
was unlawful. Good-faith consultations with

attorneys
by clients who are uncertain about the legal

implications of a proposed course of action are entitled

to the
protection of the privilege, even if that action

should
later be held improper. [page521]

The conduct
in issue
in
R. v. Campbell
was criminal

conduct.
However, the adoption into the analysis by the

Court,
without qualification, of the words "crime or tort"

and
"unfounded claims or illegal projects" from the journal

article
referred to leads, in my opinion, to the conclusions

that the
Court had in mind the proper delimitation of the

scope of the
rule and that it does not consider that

"unlawful conduct" is confined strictly to criminal and

fraudulent
conduct.

[
42
] As I
understand K.J. Smith J.'s analysis, it advances

the proposition
that if it can be shown that the client

communicated with
a lawyer with the intention of committing an

unlawful act, be
it criminal or [tortious], because the client

knew or ought to
have known that the intended conduct was

unlawful, then
the communication with the lawyer is not

privileged.
See
also:
McIntosh Estates Ltd. v. Surrey (City)
,

[1996] B.C.J. No.
2008
,
65 A.C.W.S. (3d) 736 (S.C.)
, affd

1997 CanLII 3117 (BC CA)
,
[1997] B.C.J. No.
2030
,
52 B.C.L.R. (3d) 277 (C.A.)
.

[
43
] However, a
mere assertion that the lawyer's advice was

sought in
furtherance of an illegal purpose would not be

sufficient; some
convincing evidence of the illegal purpose is

required: Re
Whitworth,
[1919] 1 Ch. 320 (C.A.)
, affd [1920]

A.C. 581,
[1920]
All E.R. Rep 1 (H.L.)
(sub nom. O'Rourke v.

Darbishire); Re
Goodman and Carr and Minister of National

Revenue,
1968 CanLII 340 (ON HCJ)
,
[1968] 2
O.R. 814
,
[1968] O.J. No. 1248 (H.C.J.)
; Blue

Line Hockey
Acquisition Co. v. Orca Bay Hockey Ltd., [2007]

B.C.J. No. 179,

155 A.C.W.S. (3d) 40 (S.C.)
; Goldman, Sachs &

Co. v. Sessions,
supra; Nanaimo Immigrant Settlement Society v.

British Columbia,

[2003] B.C.J. No. 2305
,
126 A.C.W.S. (3d) 765

(S.C.). The party
challenging lawyer-and-client privilege on

the grounds of
fraud or criminal activity must make out a prima

facie case of
fraud before the privilege is lost: Re Whitworth,

supra; Sperry
Corp. v. John Deere Ltd.,
[1984] A.C.F. no 1145
,

1984 CanLII 5875 (FC)
,
82 C.P.R. (2d) 1
(F.C.T.D.)
; Silverman v. Morresi, [1982] O.J.

No. 2266,
28
C.P.C. 239 (S.C.)
.

[
44
] In my
opinion, the exception for communications to

facilitate the
commission of a crime or a fraud applies to the

circumstances of
the case at bar, which concern the commission

of various
intentional torts against Dr. Dublin and his son.

[
45
] The e-mail
communication, which I have read, may -- and

I emphasize the
word "may" -- because the point remains to be

proven -- show
that the defendants, or at least the author of

the e-mail
message, intended to inflict emotional harm on Dr.

Dublin and his
family.

[
46
] There are
other more benign interpretations of the e-

mail, but, in my
opinion, there is enough here to rule that

the e-mail falls
within the exception to privilege for

communications in
furtherance of unlawful conduct. [page522]

[
47
] I
acknowledge, however, that my conclusion may be

contentious. In
Rocking Chair Plaza (Bramalea) Ltd. v. Brampton

(City),
[1988]
B.C.J. No. 1286
,
29 C.P.C. (2d) 82 (H.C.J.)
,

which is a case
decided before
R. v. Campbell
, supra, the

plaintiffs asked
that the fraud exception be extended to

include
communications between solicitor and client that

facilitated acts
of negligence, malicious prosecution, abuse of

process and
Charter violation. Relying on the English case,

Crescent Farms
(Sidcup) Sports Ltd. v. Sterling Officers Ltd.,

[1972] 1 Ch. 533
,

[1971] 3 All E.R. 1192
, O'Driscoll J.

refused to extend
generally the ambit of the exception for

communications in
furtherance of unlawful conduct to cover all

torts.

[
48
] However,
O'Driscoll J. defined fraud to include all

forms of fraud
and dishonesty such as fraudulent breaches of

trust, fraudulent
conspiracy, trickery and sham contrivances.

As already noted,
the Dublins in the case at bar sue for breach

of trust.

[
49
] In
Hallstone Products Ltd. v. Canada (Customs and

Revenue Agency),

[2004] O.J. No. 496
,
[2004] O.T.C. 72

(S.C.J.), Master
Dash decided that while the ambit of the

exception for
communications in furtherance of unlawful conduct

did not extend to
all torts, it did extend to acts that were an

abuse of the
court's process including abuse of the criminal

process,
deliberate suppression of evidence, and malicious

prosecution for
an improper purpose.

[
50
] I conclude
that the exception to privilege for

communications in
furtherance of unlawful conduct applies in

the immediate
case and, therefore, the e-mail message is not

privileged, and
as the e-mail is relevant, it should be

disclosed to the
plaintiffs. It follows that on this ground the

Dublins' appeal
should be allowed.

Other Grounds of
Appeal -- The E-Mail Did Not Qualify as a

Privileged
Communication

[
51
] The
Dublins advanced other grounds of appeal to

challenge the
ruling of Master Albert. As I noted at the outset

of these reasons,
I would not have allowed the appeal on these

grounds.

[
52
] As already
noted above, to qualify for lawyer-and-client

privilege, a
communication must be: (1) between a client and

his or her lawyer
who must be acting in a professional capacity

as a lawyer; (2)
given in the context of obtaining legal

advice; and (3)
intended to be confidential.

[
53
] The
Dublins argued that the communication with Mr.

Steinberg was for
non-legal business or operational advice

about the
school's infrastructure and accordingly did not

qualify as a
privileged communication.

[
54
] This type
of argument was addressed by H.J. Holmes J. in

Reid v. British
Columbia (Egg Marketing Board), [2006] B.C.J.

No. 464,
148
A.C.W.S. (3d) 878 (S.C.)
. [page523] He stated at

para. 12 of his
reasons for decision:

Not
everything said by a lawyer to a client attracts

solicitor-client privilege: Pritchard v. Ontario (Human

Rights
Commission) at para. 20. However, the protection of

solicitor-client privilege is not restricted to legal advice

relating to
interpretations of the law; it also protects

advice as to
the appropriate conduct to take in a given legal

context. The
Federal Court of Appeal explained this in Samson

Indian Band v.
Canada,
1995 CanLII 3602 (FCA)
,
[1995] 2 F.C. 762
, (1995) 125 D.L.R.

(4th) 294 at
para. 8:

. . . The
legal advice privilege protects all

communications, written or oral, between a solicitor and a

client that
are directly related to the seeking,

formulating
or giving of legal advice; it is not necessary

that the
communication specifically request or offer

advice, as
long as it can be placed within the continuum of

communication
in which the solicitor tenders advice; it is

not confined
to telling the client the law and it includes

advice as to
what should be done in the relevant legal

context.

[
55
] In my
opinion, the same reasoning applies to the

circumstances of
the case at bar. But for its tainted content,

the communication
with Mr. Steinberg would have qualified as a

communication for
the purpose of obtaining legal advice.

[
56
] Next, the
Dublins argued that given the circumstances of

its creation, the
e-mail was not intended to be confidential or

the
confidentiality was waived intentionally or recklessly and

thus the e-mail
message does not qualify as privileged.

[
57
] The master
made findings of fact against these

contentions. (See
paras. 20 to 22 of her endorsement.) In my

opinion, the
master did not err in these findings.

[
58
] I also
conclude that the master made no error in

refusing to admit
the affidavit of Neil Turner, who apparently

would have
provided expert evidence about the confidentiality

of the e-mail resident
on Ms. Nashman's computer. It appears to

me that the
Dublins were essentially fishing for information to

develop another
factual basis to assert that the e-mail was not

confidential. In
my opinion, the master made no reviewable

error in the exercise
of her discretion not to receive Mr.

Turner's
affidavit.

Other Grounds of
Appeal -- The E-mail Was Not Privileged

Because Dr.
Dublin Was a Member of the Board of Directors

[
59
] The
Dublins submit that the e-mail was not privileged

because a
corporate director is entitled to disclosure of his

or her board's
communications and Dr. Dublin was a member of

the board of
directors. Further, they argue that if there is an

exception to this
rule when there is a conflict between the

corporation and a
board member, then the exception does not

apply in the
circumstances of this case because there was no

conflict between
Dr. Dublin and the school at the time of the

e-mail. [page524]

[
60
] Dealing
with the second point first, since the Dublins

assert that the
e-mail is evidence of malice and bad faith by

the school toward
Dr. Dublin, it is inconsistent for them to

assert that there
was no conflict between the school and Dr.

Dublin at the
time of the communication with Mr. Steinberg.

Moreover, in
making the inquiry, Ms. Nashman was acting in the

interests of the
school and not necessarily in the interests of

Dr. Dublin. Thus,
there was a conflict or the potential of one,

and the point to
address is whether notwithstanding this

conflict, Dr.
Dublin is categorically entitled to disclosure of

the board's
privileged communications simply by virtue of his

status as a
director of the corporation.

[
61
] Dealing
then with the first point of whether board

communications
with a lawyer for advice about a member of the

board
categorically cannot be privileged because a board member

is normally
entitled to disclosure of all board communications,

the decision of
Ground J. in Re Livent Inc., [1999] O.J. No.

5981,
1999
CarswellOnt 4838 (S.C.J.)
addresses this point.

Ground J. refers
to his decision in Re Livent Inc. and applies

it in Hamilton v.
Pietrobon,
[2005] O.J. No. 5212
, 144 A.C.W.S.

(3d) 228
(S.C.J.).

[
62
] In Re
Livent Inc., in a reductio ad absurdum argument,

Ground J. points
out that it would lead to a ludicrous result

if a director as
litigant could negate his or her corporation's

privilege in
precisely the circumstances when the privilege is

necessary;
namely, when the corporation is seeking confidential

legal advice
about its legal relationship with the particular

director.

[
63
] I do not
dispute that a director is normally entitled to

full disclosure
of communications made to and by the board of

directors of
which he or she is a member. However, it makes

sense to qualify
that entitlement in circumstances where the

subject matter of
the communication is legal advice about the

relationship
between the director and the corporation.

[
64
] I,
therefore, conclude that this ground of appeal does

not succeed.

Other Grounds of
Appeal -- The Master Failed to Exercise her

Discretion with
respect to the Treatment of an Inadvertently

Disclosed
Privileged Document

[
65
] A line of
case law has developed to address the problem

of how the court
should respond to circumstances when a

privileged
document is inadvertently disclosed. See: Chan v.

Dynasty Executive
Suites Ltd.,
[2006] O.J. No. 2877
, 30 C.P.C.

(6th) 270
(S.C.J.); Kennedy v. McKenzie, [2005] O.J. No.

2060,
[2005]
O.T.C. 385 (S.C.J.)
; Nova Growth v. Kepinksi,

[2001] O.J. No.
5993
,
[2001] O.T.C. 1037 (S.C.J.)
; Elliott

v. Toronto (City)

(2001),
2001 CanLII 28070 (ON SC)
,
54 O.R. (3d) 472
, [2001] O.J. No.

5784 (S.C.J.);
[page525] Aviaco International Leasing Inc. v.

Boeing Canada
Inc.,
2000 CanLII 22777 (ON SC)
,
[2000] O.J. No. 2420
,
[2000] O.T.C. 982

(S.C.J.); Avenza
Global Technologies Corp. v. Cue Network

Ltd.,
[2000] O.J.
No. 1524
,
[2000] O.T.C. 285 (S.C.J.)
; Airst

v. Airst
(1998),

1998 CanLII 14647 (ON CTGD)
,
37 O.R. (3d) 654
,
[1998] O.J. No. 2615
(Gen.

Div.); Agrico
Canada Ltd. v. Stewart, Smith (Canada) Ltd.

(Insurers &
Underwriters of),
[1994] O.J. No. 2334
, 35

C.P.C. (3d) 370
(Gen. Div.);
Tilley v. Hails
(1993), 12 O.R.

(3d) 306,
1993 CanLII 8557 (ON CTGD)
,
[1993]
O.J. No. 333 (Gen. Div.)
.

[
66
] For these
circumstances of inadvertent disclosure of

privileged
documents, the case law establishes that the court

should consider a
variety of factors to determine whether steps

should be taken
to restore the privilege to the extent possible

or to treat the
privilege as waived.

[
67
] The
factors to consider when there has been inadvertent

disclosure of a
privileged document include: (a) the manner in

which the
document came to be disclosed; (b) the timing of the

inadvertent
disclosure; (c) the timing of the reassertion of

privilege; (d)
the extent of the dissemination, including the

involvement of
third parties; (e) the prejudice to the party

whose privilege
has been violated; (f) the prejudice to the

party who would
benefit by the disclosure; and (g) the impact

of the retention
or conversely the return of the document on

the procedural
fairness and the truth seeking functions of the

administration of
justice.
See:
Airst v. Airst
, supra; United

States of America
v. Levy,
[2001] O.J. No. 864
, 103 A.C.W.S.

(3d) 931
(S.C.J.); Bennett Mechanical Installations Ltd. v.

Toronto (Metropolitan),

[2001] O.J. No. 1777
,
[2001] O.T.C. 345

(S.C.J.); Kennedy
v. McKenzie, supra; Nova Growth v.

Kepinksi, supra;
Avenza Global Technologies Corp. v. Cue

Network Ltd.,
supra.

[
68
] The
Dublins submit that the master erred because she did

not consider the
factors. This submission, however, is not

correct.
Paragraph 24 of her Endorsement, while not an

elaborate
treatment, shows that the master was well aware of

how to exercise
the court's discretion in the circumstances of

the inadvertent
disclosure of privileged document.

[
69
] Having
regard to her finding that the e-mail message was

inadvertently
disclosed and assuming that the e-mail message

was privileged, I
conclude that the master made no reviewable

error in the
exercise of her discretion to order the document
